name: Anaximander's cosmic justice
plain_explanation: Anaximander pictured the elements (fire, earth, water, treated almost as rival gods) as perpetually trying to expand their 'territory' at each other's expense, but held in check by a kind of natural law of justice that always restores balance -- for example, where fire has burned, ashes (earth) remain.
precise_definition: The doctrine, stated in Anaximander's one surviving fragment, that things 'pass away into that from which they arose... making reparation and satisfaction to one another for their injustice according to the ordering of time' -- an impersonal natural necessity keeping each element within fixed bounds.
why_it_mattered: Russell treats this as one of the most profound Greek beliefs, applying a moral-legal concept (justice, not overstepping fixed bounds) to inanimate nature, and possibly a precursor of the later scientific belief in natural law.
historical_origin: Anaximander's single surviving fragment, quoted by later doxographers.
examples: Fire leaving ashes (earth) behind after burning, restoring the balance it had disturbed
influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell notes a similar conception of cosmic justice recurs in Heraclitus.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Explicitly bridges Greek legal/moral vocabulary ('justice', 'according to the ordering of time') and physical cosmology; the gods themselves are said to be subject to this impersonal justice.
